rationale: I'm replacing the 5 coarse relative bands with a finer log relative spectrum in 2 Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz, and adding each channel's log total power (1–45 Hz). Clinical abnormality in EEG shows up as specific spectral shapes: slowing focused in delta or theta, a slowed or missing posterior alpha peak, and beta from medication. Overall amplitude also changes. Coarse relative bands hide all of these. Because the feature count grows from 95 to 437, the logistic-regression C is now chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold instead of being fixed.

I'm adding a spatial feature family: band-limited channel covariance matrices for delta, theta, alpha and beta, mapped into log-Euclidean tangent space. Each matrix is divided by its trace and shrunk before the mapping, and the result is appended to the existing spectral features. Clinical abnormalities such as focal slowing, asymmetries and disrupted posterior alpha topography live in the cross-channel structure. The per-channel spectrum cannot see that structure. Covariance and Riemannian features are among the strongest feature-based TUAB descriptors (Gemein et al. 2020), and dividing by the trace keeps them independent of amplitude scale for the external sets.

TUAB recordings are routine clinical EEGs with no artifact cleaning, so eye blinks, muscle bursts, electrode pops and ±800 µV clipping inflate both the band-power estimates and the covariances. That likely blurs the spectral slowing and topographic patterns the model relies on. I'm adding one artifact-handling change. The recording is split into 10-s epochs, and epochs that clip or have outlying broadband amplitude (robust z > 3) are rejected, keeping at least half. The spectrum then becomes the median of the clean epochs' Welch PSDs, and each band covariance becomes the mean of the clean epochs' covariances. This should also make the features more robust on the external amplifiers and clinics.

Many abnormal clinical EEGs differ from normal ones by intermittent events (bursts of rhythmic delta or theta slowing, focal slowing that comes and goes, sharp transients). The median spectrum discards these on purpose. This change adds, per channel, how much each band's log relative power varies across 2-s windows inside the clean epochs: the interquartile range for delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma, plus an upper-tail measure (90th percentile minus median) for delta and theta. That explicitly encodes the intermittent slowing that clinicians use to call a recording abnormal. Because the measures use relative power, they are independent of amplitude scale for the external sets.

Clinical "abnormal" calls work like an OR over many different signs: focal slowing in any one region, a missing or slowed alpha rhythm, or diffuse beta, for example. A purely additive logistic model captures that poorly, so I'm adding a regularized LightGBM on the same features, which can model these interactions and thresholds. Its test predictions are rank-averaged with the existing tuned logistic regression. Gemein et al. 2020 found tree ensembles on spectral and covariance features among the strongest feature-based TUAB models.

I'm adding a per-channel waveform-shape family computed on the clean 1–45 Hz epochs: Hjorth mobility and complexity, the median and 90th-percentile log kurtosis across epochs, and the median skewness. Spikes, sharp waves and other paroxysmal transients are key signs that make a clinical EEG abnormal, but they are brief and broadband, so the median spectrum and the covariances barely register them; these measures target them directly and don't depend on amplitude scale.

This splits the single 13–30 Hz covariance band into low beta (13–20 Hz) and high beta (20–30 Hz) and adds a 30–45 Hz band, so the spatial covariance features cover the full spectrum at finer resolution. Low beta often reflects drug-induced (benzodiazepine/barbiturate) diffuse beta, high beta and 30–45 Hz reflect muscle and frontal fast activity, and these have different spatial topographies. A single wide beta matrix blurs them, while the per-channel spectrum already resolves them but can't show their spatial structure.

Clinical "abnormal" calls often rest on focal slowing or a focal loss of rhythm in either hemisphere. A linear model on per-channel spectra can only learn signed left-right differences, so left-sided and right-sided focal slowing cancel out. I'm adding per-homologous-pair absolute hemispheric asymmetries |L−R| of log relative band power (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) and log total power, plus the largest asymmetry across pairs for each band. These directly encode "a focal abnormality on either side", and as differences of log-relative quantities they don't depend on amplitude scale or gain.

I'm adding a volume-conduction-insensitive connectivity family: weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) between all 171 channel pairs in each covariance band (delta, theta, alpha, beta). It is computed from the Hilbert analytic signal over the artifact-screened samples. The existing covariances only capture zero-lag coupling, which volume conduction and the reference dominate. Lagged phase coupling reflects genuine network disruption, as in encephalopathy, focal lesions and epileptiform networks. It is also unaffected by amplitude scale and reference, which matters for the external sets.

The covariance features are currently log-mapped at the identity, which distorts and couples the coordinates for matrices far from identity. I'm switching to the standard Riemannian tangent space at the training fold's geometric (affine-invariant) mean, using pyriemann TangentSpace fit on the training fold only. Each covariance is then whitened by the population reference before the log map, so the vectors measure each recording's deviation from the typical EEG spatial structure. That should make focal or topographic abnormalities easier for both the logistic regression and LightGBM to separate. The covariances are still trace-normalized, so they stay independent of amplitude scale.

The two current models are an additive linear model and axis-aligned trees. Neither captures smooth "distance from the normal EEG manifold" structure well, where an abnormal recording deviates moderately in many spectral and topographic coordinates at once. I'm adding a third member, an RBF-kernel SVM on the same standardized spectral and tangent-space features with C chosen by grouped inner CV. It enters the existing rank average with equal weight, adding kernel-based diversity (SVMs were competitive feature-based TUAB models in Gemein et al. 2020).

I'm adding explicit per-channel spectral-shape features computed from the clean-epoch median PSD (0.5-Hz resolution): the aperiodic 1/f exponent, plus a peak alpha frequency and alpha-peak height measured on the residual after removing the 1/f fit (6–14 Hz), plus the 50% and 90% spectral edge frequencies (SEF50, SEF90). Clinicians call a recording abnormal when the posterior dominant rhythm is slowed (below about 8.5 Hz) or missing, or when the overall spectrum is shifted toward slow frequencies. The 2-Hz relative bins can represent these only indirectly and too coarsely. These new features are nonlinear summaries that don't depend on amplitude scale, and all three models can use them directly.

Every current model sees only one summary per recording (a median spectrum and a mean covariance). That throws away the epoch-to-epoch variation that clinicians read: intermittent slowing or short bursts of abnormal activity. It also leaves only about 2,200 training rows. I'm adding a fourth ensemble member: a LightGBM trained on the per-epoch spectra of the clean 10-s epochs (about 30 per recording, each labeled with its recording's label). Its epoch log-odds are averaged per recording, the same crop-and-aggregate idea behind the strongest deep-net results on TUAB, and the result joins the existing rank average with equal weight.

Clinicians judge the posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) on eyes-closed, relaxed stretches. The REST recordings mix eyes-open and eyes-closed, so the median spectrum mostly reflects eyes-open activity and blurs out a slowed or missing PDR. For each recording I select the 25% of clean epochs with the highest posterior (O/P channels) 7–13 Hz relative power, as a proxy for eyes-closed segments. From those epochs I add their median log relative spectrum (2-Hz bins, 1–21 Hz) per channel as a state-matched spectral block. These features use relative power only, so they stay independent of amplitude scale.
